title: Optimal Dynamic Pricing of Inventories with Stochastic Demand over Finite Horizons
research_question: How should a seller dynamically price fixed perishable inventory under stochastic price-sensitive demand?
data: Theoretical model; numerical illustrations
method: Continuous-time stochastic dynamic control and heuristics
main_result: Optimal prices balance current revenue against the opportunity cost of capacity; the framework permits random cancellations but does not model weather-driven reliability risk.
relevance: Foundational link from demand and remaining capacity to prices.
gap_relative_to_project: No observed airline fares, ex-ante operational-risk measure, or risk-by-demand pricing interaction.

title: A Multiproduct Dynamic Pricing Problem and Its Applications to Network Yield Management
research_question: How should a capacity-constrained network price multiple products sharing resources?

main_result: Prices and availability depend on network opportunity costs and demand intensities.
relevance: Provides the core revenue-management logic behind fare-class availability and demand-responsive pricing.

title: Using Yield Management to Shift Demand When the Peak Time is Unknown
research_question: Can price dispersion and rationed low-fare availability efficiently shift demand when the peak period is unknown?
data: Theoretical model motivated by airlines and other perishable-capacity industries
method: Competitive equilibrium model with aggregate uncertainty and price rigidities
main_result: Multiple prices and restricted low-price availability can shift demand and reduce capacity costs even without knowing which period will peak.
relevance: Shows why demand uncertainty and capacity constraints can produce dispersion without product-quality differences.
gap_relative_to_project: Uncertainty concerns peak demand, not forecast operational failure; no risk-by-demand slope estimate.
verification_level: full text verified via journal copy; bibliographic metadata verified
notes: Primary journal article; stable JSTOR URL.

title: Competition and Price Dispersion in the U.S. Airline Industry
research_question: How much within-carrier route fare dispersion exists and how does it vary with competition?
data: U.S. passenger ticket records aggregated by carrier-route
method: Cross-sectional econometric analysis of fare dispersion
main_result: The expected absolute fare difference between two passengers on a route averaged 36% of the mean fare; dispersion was higher on more competitive routes and routes with lower flight density.
relevance: Establishes large cross-sectional airfare dispersion in ticket data similar in spirit to DB1B.
gap_relative_to_project: Quarterly ticket data do not reveal quote timing, inventory, forecast risk, or why a given fare changed.
verification_level: authoritative NBER abstract/full working paper and published-version metadata verified
notes: Published version identified by NBER.

title: Price Discrimination in the Airline Market: The Effect of Market Concentration
research_question: How do ticket restrictions and market concentration affect airline price discrimination?
data: U.S. route fares and ticket restrictions
method: Econometric analysis controlling for distance and gate restrictions
main_result: Advance-purchase and Saturday-night-stay restrictions carry price effects, and measured price discrimination increases with competition in the studied sample.
relevance: Directly demonstrates that fare restrictions and fare classes encode product differentiation, not just a single price.
gap_relative_to_project: Does not isolate refund levels, exchangeability, weather risk, or flight-specific demand states.
verification_level: Federal Reserve full working paper and final-publication metadata verified
notes: Page range follows published citation in the Federal Reserve record.

title: Price Dispersion under Costly Capacity and Demand Uncertainty
research_question: Do costly capacity and uncertain demand explain airline fare dispersion?
data: Daily fares and seat inventories for 228 U.S. domestic flights over 103 days
method: Panel econometrics testing Prescott-Eden-Dana predictions
main_result: Lower selling probabilities are associated with higher prices, with a larger effect in more competitive markets; advance-purchase discount evidence remains after controlling for demand uncertainty.
relevance: Very close evidence connecting inventory/selling probability and airfare.
gap_relative_to_project: Selling probability is not operational reliability; there is no forecast weather or cancellation-risk interaction.
verification_level: NBER abstract and full working paper verified
notes: Working paper status retained; no unverified journal citation substituted.

title: Capacity-Contingent Pricing and Competition in the Airline Industry
research_question: How do own and rival remaining capacities affect posted airline prices?
data: High-frequency prices and load factors from airline websites on a busy U.S. corridor
method: Flight-level panel analysis
main_result: Some airlines respond to rival prices and load factors and raise prices as rivals' available seats disappear, even controlling for days and own seats remaining.
relevance: Shows contemporaneous capacity information can affect dynamic fare setting.
gap_relative_to_project: Capacity scarcity is not disruption probability; the analysis does not test weather/reliability risk or its interaction with demand.
verification_level: publisher abstract and bibliographic metadata verified
notes: Evidence summary limited to accessible abstract.

title: Dynamic Pricing, Advance Sales and Aggregate Demand Learning in Airlines
research_question: Do prices respond to inventory, time to departure, and newly revealed aggregate demand?
data: Panel of U.S. flight fares, inventories, and sales
method: Joint dynamic price and demand equations
main_result: Prices rise as inventory falls and fall as time to sell shrinks; demand shocks have a positive and much larger price effect than anticipated sales.
relevance: The closest verified empirical study of demand learning and fare response.
gap_relative_to_project: No ex-ante operational/weather risk measure and no test of whether risk changes the demand-price slope.
verification_level: publisher abstract/metadata and author-hosted full paper verified
notes: Primary Wiley page and author-hosted article used.

title: The Welfare Effects of Dynamic Pricing: Evidence From Airline Markets
research_question: What drives dynamic airline pricing and what are its welfare effects?
data: Novel flight-level prices and seat availability for U.S. airline markets
method: Structural dynamic demand and pricing model; counterfactual uniform pricing
main_result: Airfares respond both to demand shocks and changing willingness to pay; dynamic pricing benefits early leisure travelers and harms late business travelers relative to uniform pricing, with aggregate welfare effects varying by market.
relevance: Separates demand shocks from intertemporal consumer composition using the type of flight-level state data the original hypothesis would need.
gap_relative_to_project: Does not include weather forecasts, cancellation/delay probabilities, or operational-risk interactions.
verification_level: publisher abstract and metadata verified; NBER working paper available
notes: The earlier title was Dynamic Airline Pricing and Seat Availability.

authors: Thomas Fiig; Remy Le Guen; Mathilde Gauchet
title: Dynamic Pricing of Airline Offers
venue: Journal of Revenue and Pricing Management 17(6):381-393
research_question: How can airlines move from filed booking-class fares to dynamically priced offers including ancillaries and flexibility?
data: Industry systems description and illustrative optimization formulations
method: Practice article; conceptual architecture and pricing formulations
main_result: A continuous optimal offer price combines bid price/opportunity cost with a choice model; existing booking classes and fare rules limit price granularity, while flexibility and fare-lock products create further pricing problems.
relevance: Primary bridge to continuous pricing, fare families, flexibility products, and contextual attributes; it explicitly lists destination weather forecast as a possible ancillary-pricing attribute.
gap_relative_to_project: No causal or observational evidence that weather forecasts affect base fares; no operational-risk-by-demand test.
verification_level: full publisher-version PDF verified
notes: Full text hosted by IATA; bibliographic details and DOI visible in the article.

authors: Daniel Garcia; Maarten C. W. Janssen; Radostina Shopova
title: Dynamic Pricing with Uncertain Capacities
research_question: How does private information about rivals' unsold capacities affect dynamic pricing for time-dated products?
data: Theoretical two-firm model with extensions motivated by airlines and hotels
method: Dynamic equilibrium analysis
main_result: Private capacity information can generate price dispersion and rising expected prices near the deadline while limiting market power; information exchange can raise firms' profits.
relevance: Provides a clean supply-uncertainty pricing mechanism adjacent to operational-risk pricing.
gap_relative_to_project: Uncertain rival capacity differs from uncertain service delivery; baseline demand is known and there is no airline weather evidence.

title: The Effect of Air Traffic Delays on Airline Prices
research_question: How does an exogenous increase in delays affect airline prices?
data: U.S. route fares and delays around a change in LaGuardia takeoff/landing restrictions
method: Quasi-experimental econometric analysis
main_result: Prices fell by about $1.42 for each additional minute of delay, with a larger response in more competitive markets.
relevance: Strong causal evidence that realized/experienced reliability quality can affect market fares.
gap_relative_to_project: The shock is route quality, not quote-time forecast weather risk; it estimates a fare level response, not risk-by-demand slope moderation.

authors: Rodrigo Britto; Martin Dresner; Augusto Voltes
title: The Impact of Flight Delays on Passenger Demand and Societal Welfare
research_question: How do route delays affect passenger demand, airfares, and welfare?
data: U.S. route-level traffic, fares, and lagged delay measures
method: Simultaneous demand and fare equations estimated by two-stage least squares; welfare calculations
main_result: Route delays reduce passenger demand and raise average fares in the study, consistent with demand and cost channels; both consumer and producer welfare fall.
relevance: Jointly models delay, demand, and fare, making it one of the closest aggregate precedents.
gap_relative_to_project: Uses lagged realized delay as route quality/cost, not ex-ante flight risk; does not estimate delay-risk × demand in the fare equation.

title: Flight Delay Impact on Airfare and Flight Frequency: A Comprehensive Assessment
research_question: How do origin, destination, and hub delays affect U.S. airfares and flight frequency?
data: U.S. itinerary-level fares, schedule/frequency, airport delays, cost, demand, and competition characteristics

authors: Jane Lee; Lavanya Marla; Alexandre Jacquillat
title: Dynamic Disruption Management in Airline Networks Under Airport Operating Uncertainty
research_question: Can airlines combine probabilistic airport-congestion forecasts with reactive recovery decisions?
data: Airport queueing estimates, Boeing/Jeppesen flight planning, and airline network experiments
method: Stochastic queuing plus dynamic stochastic integer programming; look-ahead and sample-average approximation
main_result: Using partial probabilistic forecasts reduced expected recovery costs by 1%-2% versus a myopic realized-disruption baseline in experiments.
relevance: Shows ex-ante operating uncertainty is measurable and decision-relevant within airline operations.
gap_relative_to_project: Optimizes recovery actions and costs, not customer fares; no demand-price interaction.

title: Conditional Efficiency, Operational Risk and Electronic Ticket Pricing Strategies for the Airline Industry
venue: International Journal of Electronic Marketing and Retailing 2(3):239-255
research_question: How can operational risk metrics compare discount-ticket pricing strategies?
data: Stylized 150-seat regional-airline case; focus-group price-response inputs; simulated demand
method: Monte Carlo simulation; operational value at risk and expected shortfall; conditional-efficient frontier
main_result: The model selects discount size and seat allocation by expected profit and downside profit risk, allowing recapture between fare classes.
relevance: Terminologically close and relevant to pricing under uncertainty.
gap_relative_to_project: Operational risk means the distribution of profit caused mainly by uncertain demand and input assumptions, not weather/delay/cancellation risk. It is simulated, not an observed risk × demand effect on fare quotes.
verification_level: publisher metadata and author-uploaded full text verified
notes: This paper prevents an unqualified claim that operational risk and airline ticket pricing have never been linked.
